title: Real-time audio pipeline engineering
subtitle: PCM framing, resampling, echo-cancellation reference, pacing and drop-on-reconnect: the audio path from a desk microphone or a Teams call to my own speech models.

lede: In Helix I wanted one voice engine to work on a desk microphone and inside a Teams call without the conversation logic knowing which. I gave the Rust engine one sealed audio seam: an abstract source and sink with one frame contract, so a new audio endpoint is an implementation and the engine does not change. The same turn-taking and interruption behaviour runs in both. The front end is a chain of stages over that frame contract, each reading and writing the same frames.
quote: An agent acting on words nobody said is worse than one that asks again.
evidence: Real-time voice AI: one Rust voice engine behind a sealed audio seam of 20 ms frames, 16 kHz in and 24 kHz out, on a desk microphone and inside Teams calls.
Microsoft Teams real-time media: a .NET media bridge and Rust host on one WebSocket per call, a 30-minute soak moving 91,643 buffers at 50.001 per second with 0 receive stalls.
Audio signal processing: echo cancellation, a denoiser under a 30 ms 95th-percentile latency gate, an operator voiceprint filter and voice-activity detection ahead of recognition.
Latency engineering: question-to-first-sound cut from about 2.1 s to about 0.9 s with streaming synthesis and cached voice conditioning.
author: Corey James
